# Flushing Engine Coolant After Oil Intrusion

Oil in your cooling system isn't just a messy stain; it fundamentally alters the chemical and physical properties of the coolant. When oil mixes with ethylene glycol-based antifreeze, it creates an emulsion that appears as a milky, chocolate-milk sludge. This mixture loses its ability to transfer heat efficiently because oil is a poor thermal conductor compared to water or glycol. For your 2002 Buick LeSabre with the new motor, water pump, and thermostat, simply draining the block once will not restore system integrity. The oil has likely coated internal passages in the cylinder head, the intake manifold gasket area, and potentially the new water pump bearings.

The primary objective of a flush is to remove this contamination without introducing air pockets or stripping protective coatings off metal surfaces that don't need them. You cannot rely on gravity drainage alone. Oil adheres tenaciously to wet surfaces due to surface tension. To effectively clear the system, you need to circulate a solvent that breaks down the oil-glycol bond before draining it out completely.

### Selecting the Right Flush Agent

The first step is choosing an appropriate flush chemical. Do not use standard water or a weak detergent mixture; these will merely redistribute the sludge and potentially clog the new radiator cap seal or the thermostat housing. Instead, opt for a dedicated engine flush concentrate designed to break down oil emulsions. These products typically contain surfactants that lower surface tension, allowing the fluid to slide off oily surfaces and carry it out through the drain plugs.

If you prefer a mechanical approach without chemicals, high-pressure water flushing is an option but carries significant risk. You must avoid using a pressure washer directly into the radiator neck. The sudden pressure spike can force oil deeper into narrow passages or damage the delicate seals of the new water pump and thermostat. If you proceed with water, use a garden hose at low pressure (under 40 PSI) and rely on gravity to pull fluid through.

### The Flushing Procedure

Begin by ensuring the engine is completely cool to prevent thermal shock to the new aluminum components. Locate all drain plugs on the radiator and the lower engine block. Remove these carefully, noting that some engines have a small oil cooler line that drains into the bottom of the radiator; this line must be disconnected and drained separately to ensure no residual sludge remains in the oil circuit.

Pour your chosen flush concentrate into the coolant reservoir or directly into the radiator neck up to the fill line. Start the engine and let it idle until it reaches operating temperature. Watch for steam rising from the exhaust; this indicates the thermostat has opened, allowing the new water pump to circulate fluid through the entire system, including the heater core.

Once the engine warms up, let it run for about 10 to 15 minutes. This circulation time is critical to loosen the emulsified oil clinging to the cylinder walls and the new pump internals. Do not rev the engine excessively, as this can agitate the sludge into a thicker paste that is harder to remove. After the timer expires, turn off the engine and allow it to cool slightly so the fluid doesn't spray when you open the radiator cap. Drain the contaminated flush mixture completely.

### Verification and Refill

After draining the first batch, inspect the color of the liquid in the drain pan. If it is still dark brown or milky, repeat the process with a fresh batch of flush concentrate until the drained fluid runs clear. This iterative step is where many owners cut corners, but given the severity of oil intrusion, multiple passes are often necessary to ensure no microscopic droplets remain.

Once the system is flushed clear, refill it with the correct mixture of antifreeze and distilled water according to the manufacturer's specifications for your LeSabre. Never use tap water, as the minerals can form scale over time, negating the benefits of the flush. Bleed the air from the system thoroughly by running the engine with the radiator cap off until the thermostat opens and a steady stream of coolant flows without bubbles.

Finally, check the oil filler cap and dipstick. If any milky residue appears in the crankcase oil after a few hundred miles, there may be a compromised head gasket allowing combustion gases or more oil to enter the system, requiring further investigation beyond a simple flush.
